input_text:
2.4 Legal Readymade

In this section, we will explore the idea of legal readymades – the ways in which existing laws can be used as tools or building blocks to question, critique, or even disrupt data collection systems. This concept draws its name from Marcel Duchamp’s “readymades” – ordinary objects he selected and presented as art, thereby transforming their meaning and function. Similarly, lawyers and activists repurpose existing laws to challenge data practices, turning them into powerful instruments for social change.

A. Privacy Laws and Their Limitations

Privacy laws aim to protect individuals from unauthorized intrusions into their private lives. However, these laws often struggle to keep up with rapid technological advancements and changing societal norms around privacy. In many cases, they leave loopholes that allow companies to collect vast amounts of personal information without explicit consent.

For instance, consider the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), one of the most comprehensive privacy regulations worldwide. GDPR grants people several rights related to their personal data, such as the right to access, rectify, erase, restrict processing, object to processing, and data portability. Yet, despite these protections, tech giants still find ways to exploit users’ data through sophisticated surveillance techniques and complex terms of service agreements.

B. Repurposing Copyright Laws for Data Privacy

One creative strategy to address gaps in privacy legislation involves using copyright law as a tool for protecting personal information. While copyright primarily deals with artistic creations rather than individual privacy, artists and advocates have found inventive ways to leverage it against invasive data collection practices.

Artist Paolo Cirio’s project “Loophole for All” exemplifies this approach. Cirio discovered that companies listed on the New York Stock Exchange were required by law to publish annual reports containing sensitive financial data. He then wrote a computer program that scraped this information from SEC filings and sold it back to the same corporations at exorbitant prices. By doing so, Cirio highlighted the absurdity of lax data protection rules and demonstrated how copyright could serve as a weapon against unwanted disclosures.

C. Contract Law and Terms of Service

Another way to interrogate data collection systems is through contract law, specifically examining the fine print of terms of service agreements. These lengthy documents often contain clauses that grant companies extensive rights over user data, sometimes even allowing them to sell it to third parties without prior notification or consent.

However, not all hope is lost. Some consumers have successfully challenged oppressive terms of service provisions in court, leading to more balanced agreements. Furthermore, organizations like the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) advocate for transparency and fairness in online contracts, pushing policymakers to enact stronger consumer protections.

D. Litigation as Advocacy

Lawsuits can also serve as powerful catalysts for reform. When brought strategically, they raise public awareness about problematic data practices and force companies to reconsider their policies. Moreover, successful litigation often results in significant monetary settlements, which may deter future violations and fund further advocacy efforts.

For instance, in 2018, Facebook agreed to pay $5 billion to settle Federal Trade Commission charges relating to its improper sharing of user data with Cambridge Analytica. Although this amount pales compared to Facebook’s revenue, it remains one of the largest penalties ever imposed on a technology company for privacy violations.

E. Conclusion

Legal readymades offer exciting opportunities to engage critically with data collection systems and push back against corporate overreach. By understanding the potential applications and limitations of various laws, students can become informed participants in shaping our digital landscape. Through creativity, persistence, and strategic thinking, young people can help ensure that technology serves society’s needs while respecting individual autonomy and dignity.
